analysis.one_liner: Bans contract terms that stop health plans from steering patients to cheaper, higher-quality providers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a Republican and a Democratic senator, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban health systems and hospital networks from writing contract terms that limit competition. Insurers and employer health plans could not be forced to cover a hospital's affiliates, accept rates for entities outside the contract, or be blocked from steering patients to lower-cost, higher-quality doctors and facilities. The idea is that large hospital systems use these terms to keep prices high, and banning them would lower what patients and employers pay for care.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and employers would gain if banned terms mean plans can steer enrollees to lower-cost, higher-quality providers instead of being locked into a hospital system's entire network and rates. Insurers and self-insured employers gain bargaining power, since contracts could no longer bind them to affiliate deals or rates for parties they never agreed to. Self-insured employers would also get disclosure when a third-party administrator binds them to restrictive terms they never signed.

how_it_helps.text: Bans four kinds of anticompetitive contract terms: restrictions on steering enrollees to specific providers, requirements to contract with a provider's affiliates, requirements to accept payment rates for entities not party to the contract, and clauses barring other plans from negotiating lower rates.

Requires disclosure to self-insured employers when a third-party administrator has bound them to restrictive contracting terms they were never party to, a situation that can otherwise stay hidden from the employer paying the bills.

Preserves plans' ability to design narrower, value-based networks, tier providers by cost and quality, and steer enrollees to centers of excellence, which is how plans try to deliver cheaper, higher-quality care.

analysis.who_pays: Large hospital systems and provider networks would lose contract terms that lock insurers into paying for their affiliates and block plans from steering patients elsewhere, reducing their leverage to negotiate high prices. Health insurers and plans would bear a modest compliance cost from filing an annual attestation of compliance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large hospital systems and provider networks

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out broad exceptions: group-model HMOs operating through exclusive contracts with multi-specialty physician groups, and value-based arrangements like accountable care organizations, exclusive provider networks, and centers of excellence, are exempt from the steering ban, so many of the contracts with restrictive terms could continue under those labels.
Compliance relies on annual attestations by plans and issuers to federal regulators rather than on new penalties or audits, which may limit how much the ban changes real-world contracting.

Allowing plans to steer enrollees with incentives cuts both ways: plans gain flexibility to negotiate lower prices, but patients could face pressure to use certain providers even when they prefer their current doctor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real but bounded: the four banned terms are genuine tools that consolidated hospital systems use to keep prices high, and banning them would strengthen plans' and employers' negotiating position. The cost falls mainly on large provider systems' negotiating leverage, plus minor paperwork for plans. The bill's own exceptions for HMOs and value-based arrangements, and its reliance on attestations rather than enforcement, mean its practical effect would likely be narrower than its headline.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Braun introduced the bill on November 2, 2021, with Senator Tammy Baldwin as its sole cosponsor, making it a bipartisan two-senator effort.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; no further action was ever recorded.
It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action, and expired with the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large hospital systems and provider networks keep the contract terms that lock insurers into paying for their affiliates and stop plans from steering patients to cheaper providers. Employers and patients continue paying prices shaped by those terms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large hospital systems keep their leverage

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining a Republican sponsor on a health-competition measure.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held.

against.name: Sen. Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule the bill for a committee hearing or markup during the two years it was pending.

sides.party_line_note: The only record is a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor; with no votes or committee action, the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: Hospital systems and consolidated provider networks
industries.note: The bill strips hospital systems of contract terms that force insurers to cover their affiliates, accept rates for entities outside the contract, and block plans from steering patients elsewhere. Those terms are how large systems convert market power into higher prices, so their loss would be patients' and employers' gain.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Plans and self-insured employers gain bargaining freedom: no affiliate-contract mandates, no most-favored-rate clauses, and full ability to steer enrollees to lower-cost, higher-quality providers. They take on a small compliance cost from annual attestations.

industries.industry: Group-model HMOs and value-based care networks
industries.note: The bill exempts group-model HMOs with exclusive physician-group contracts and value-based arrangements like ACOs and centers of excellence, leaving their exclusive contracts untouched. This softens the bill's impact and reflects these networks' established place in the system.
